name: Canon and Interpretation

objectives.text: Name the two main parts of the Bible as the Old Testament and the New Testament
Identify that the Bible is made up of 66 books written by many human authors over a long period of time
Locate a passage in the Bible by book, chapter, and verse using the table of contents
Sort the books of the Bible into their main groups such as Law, History, Poetry, Prophets, Gospels, and Letters
Explain that the church recognized the books God gave as Scripture rather than creating or approving them
Describe why readers sometimes need help to understand hard passages of Scripture using the account of the Ethiopian official
Explain the Reformed teaching that what must be known for salvation is clearly set forth in Scripture so ordinary readers can understand it
Summarize the marks the early church looked for in recognizing New Testament books, including apostolic origin, agreement with the faith, and wide use in the churches
Apply the rule of context by reading the surrounding verses before stating what a single verse means
Explain how Jesus and the apostles affirmed the Hebrew Scriptures as the Old Testament canon
Compare the books of the Apocrypha with the canonical books and explain why Protestant churches do not receive them as Scripture
Identify the literary genre of a passage such as narrative, poetry, prophecy, parable, or letter and explain how genre shapes the way it is read
Analyze the criteria the early church used to recognize canonical books and explain the Reformed position that the canon rests on God's self-attesting word rather than on church decree
Explain how New Testament writers quoted and interpreted the Old Testament using examples such as Jesus's teaching on the road to Emmaus
Explain why the Reformed tradition holds that the canon is closed with the completion of the apostolic foundation
Interpret a passage by examining its words, grammar, historical setting, and original audience
Distinguish the illumination of the Holy Spirit in understanding Scripture from the giving of new revelation as the Reformed tradition teaches
Explain why the Reformation churches stressed the original languages of Scripture and faithful translation into the common language
Trace the historical recognition of the canon using sources such as the Muratorian Fragment, the 39th Festal Letter of Athanasius, and the councils of Hippo and Carthage
Explain how biblical theology follows themes such as covenant and promise across the whole canon toward their fulfillment in Christ
Evaluate the claims of Gnostic and other noncanonical gospels using the historical criteria of canonicity
Evaluate modern claims of ongoing revelation in light of the Reformed doctrine of a closed canon
Apply the analogy of faith by using clearer passages of Scripture to interpret less clear ones
Compare the Reformed principle that Scripture interprets Scripture with approaches that place final interpretive authority in church tradition
Create a written exegesis of a passage that applies context, genre, grammar, and the analogy of faith

changes: Replaced every citation of Jude 3 with Jude 1:3. Kept the real competencies from the old list, reworded and regraded, including canon size, Old and New Testaments, the church recognizing the canon, how books were recognized, perspicuity, the Apocrypha, context, the closed canon, illumination, the history of the canon, Gnostic gospels, modern prophecy claims, and the analogy of faith. Removed the vague 'we need help' wording and replaced it with an objective tied to Acts 8. Moved the standalone sufficiency objective into the closed-canon objective so it does not overlap the sibling sub-topics. Added objectives on locating references, grouping the books, the Old Testament canon, genre, New Testament use of the Old Testament, grammatical-historical reading, original languages and translation, biblical theology, comparison with tradition-based interpretation, and a capstone exegesis. Confession references now use full document names, with Belgic Confession articles added where they apply.
